q-48504:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=ln⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot ln⁡x-{x}^{2}\cdot (ln⁡x)^{′}}{(ln⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{x})}{{(ln⁡(x))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-x}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & =\frac{x(2ln⁡(x)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e(2ln⁡(e)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(e)} \\  & =\frac{e(2-1)}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e.$

q-11969:
Let $u=-x$ and $v=9-2x.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =-1\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(9-2x)\cdot (-1)-(-x)\cdot (-2)}{{(9-2x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-9+2x-2x}{{(9-2x)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{(9-2x)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-4807:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=5$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,3),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(3) & =5(x-1) \\ y & =5x-5+3 \\ y & =5x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-103325:
Let $f(x)=4{x}^{3}-9x-1.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{3}-9x-1)=12{x}^{2}-9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m={f}^{′}(-1)=12(1)^{2}-9=3.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-6) & =3(x-1) \\ y & =3x-3-6 \\ y & =3x-9.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =3x-9 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $(3,0).$

q-84959:
The number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $9$ pencils in the box, so $n=9.$ We want to select $4$ of those pencils, so we have $r=4.$

Therefore, the number of different potential sets of four pencils is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{9}{C}_{4} & =\frac{9!}{(9-4)!\,4!} \\  & =\frac{9!}{5!4!} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot 6\cdot \cancel{5!}}{\cancel{5!}4!} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot 6}{4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{3\,024}{24} \\  & =126.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122560:
In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $12$ flavors, so $n=12.$ We want to select $3$ of those flavors, so we have $r=3.$

Therefore, the number of choices is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{12}{C}_{3} & =\frac{12!}{(12-3)!\,3!} \\  & =\frac{12!}{9!3!} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10\cdot \cancel{9!}}{\cancel{9!}3!} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{1\,320}{6} \\  & =220.\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, reflect it across the $y$-axis.

- Finally, stretch it parallel to the $y$-axis by a stretch factor of $5.$

Therefore, the given curve is the graph of $y=5sin⁡(-x).$

Notice that, because the sine function is odd, the $y$-axis reflection has the same effect as the $x$-axis reflection, i.e.,

$$
5sin⁡(-x)=-5sin⁡x.

q-48835:
Using the product rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x)) & =f(x){g}^{′}(x)+g(x){f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $x=e$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))|}_{x=e} & =f(e){g}^{′}(e)+g(e){f}^{′}(e) \\  & =1\cdot 2e+{e}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{e} \\  & =3e.\end{aligned}
$$

q-48836:
Using the product rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x)) & =f(x){g}^{′}(x)+g(x){f}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $x=4$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))|}_{x=4} & =f(4){g}^{′}(4)+g(4){f}^{′}(4) \\  & =(-3)\cdot \frac{1}{4}+2\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{11}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
